topic: Foundations of Linear Algebra: From Combinations to Bases

sections.title: The Ingredients: Linear Combinations and Span
sections.content: Define a linear combination as scaling and adding vectors. Explain 'Span' as the set of all possible reach points in space. Use a 2D plane animation where two vectors 'stretch' their reach across the entire surface.
sections.example: Imagine a robot arm moving in a 2D plane: if you have two motors (vectors), any point the arm can touch is the 'Span'.

sections.title: Redundancy: Linear Dependence
sections.content: Introduce the concept of 'Linear Dependence' as redundant information. Visually demonstrate two vectors lying on the same line or three vectors forming a flat plane in 3D space, showing that one vector adds no new 'reach'.
sections.example: If you have two GPS satellites (vectors) that are perfectly aligned, the second one provides no new triangulation data—it is 'linearly dependent'.

sections.title: Efficiency: The Basis
sections.content: Define a 'Basis' as the minimal set of vectors that can span the space without any redundancy (linearly independent). Emphasize that every vector in the space can be uniquely represented by a basis.
sections.example: Think of coordinates (x, y) on a map: the basis vectors are North and East. You don't need a third direction to reach any point on the map, and you can't reach all points with just one.

sections.title: Synthesis and Summary
sections.content: Recap how Span provides the reach, Independence ensures efficiency, and Basis combines both to form the 'DNA' of a vector space. Connect these to higher-dimensional applications.
sections.example: A video game designer using a 3D coordinate system (basis) to render a character's movement within a 3D environment.
